explanations.answer: At the right hand of God's throne in heaven
explanations.explanation: That's the seat, baker. The writer says Jesus took His seat at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven. He is the high priest we really do have, seated in heaven.

explanations.answer: Beside the altar in the temple courts
explanations.explanation: Close to priest territory, but the writer puts Jesus somewhere else. He sat down in heaven, at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty. Verse 4 even says that if He were on earth, He would not be a priest. So no altar-side chair for Him.

explanations.answer: On Mount Sinai with the seventy elders
explanations.explanation: A mountain does show up in this passage, but it's Moses' mountain in verse 5, where he was shown a pattern for the tabernacle. That has nothing to do with where Jesus sits. The writer says He sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven. Nice try, friend.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: The writer says the opposite. Jesus ministers in the sanctuary and true tabernacle “…set up by the Lord, not by man.” No human builder set it up. My mustache can barely set up a cookie rack without a wobble.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The sanctuary and true tabernacle where Jesus ministers was “…set up by the Lord, not by man.” The writer states it plainly. This one wasn't built by a crew with hammers.

explanations.answer: Offer both gifts and sacrifices
explanations.explanation: That's the job. The writer says “…every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices…” It's the reason he says Jesus needed something to offer too. A priest without an offering would be like me showing up with an empty cookie box.

explanations.answer: Guard the ark of the covenant
explanations.explanation: The ark is a holy thing, but this verse doesn't give it to the high priest as his job. The writer says every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices. That's the whole description in this verse.

explanations.answer: Lead the army into battle
explanations.explanation: Nothing about armor in this job description, friend. The writer says every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices. That's what the appointment is for, in this verse.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: The writer says it the other way around. He says, “Now if He were on earth, He would not be a priest…” The reason he gives is that there are already priests who offer gifts according to the law. So Jesus' priestly work isn't a job on earth's roster.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The writer says if Jesus were on earth, He would not be a priest. The reason given is that there are already priests here who offer gifts according to the law. Jesus has received a much more excellent ministry, the writer says in verse 6.

explanations.answer: A copy and shadow of what is in heaven
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says the place where they serve is “…a copy and shadow of what is in heaven.” A copy points to the real thing without being the real thing. The real thing is what is in heaven.

explanations.answer: A gate that opens straight into heaven
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't call it a gate. He calls the place where the earthly priests serve a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. A copy isn't a doorway. It points to something real.

explanations.answer: A throne room filled with heaven's glory
explanations.explanation: The throne is in heaven, where Jesus sat down (Hebrews 8:1). The earthly place is described as a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. The writer doesn't call it a throne room.

explanations.answer: The pattern shown him on the mountain
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses, Israel's leader, was warned, “…make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.” The warning came when he was about to build the tabernacle.

explanations.answer: The design King David gave Solomon
explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king, did give his son Solomon plans for the temple (1 Chronicles 28:11). But Moses was warned about the tabernacle, and the pattern he followed was the one shown him on the mountain. Different builder, different building.

explanations.answer: The measurements shown Ezekiel in a vision
explanations.explanation: Ezekiel, a prophet, did see a vision of a temple (Ezekiel 40:2). That's a different person and a different building from Moses and the tabernacle. Moses had to make everything according to the pattern shown him on the mountain.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True, baker. The writer says Jesus has received a more excellent ministry, “…just as the covenant He mediates is better and is founded on better promises.” Better ministry, better covenant, better promises. And we haven't even gotten to the promises yet.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Actually, the writer says it plainly. The covenant Jesus mediates “…is better and is founded on better promises.” So this one is true. Hold on to that word 'promises,' because the next stop is full of them.

explanations.answer: people
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says, “But God found fault with the people…” That's who God found fault with. Verse 7 adds that if the first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second.

explanations.answer: prophets
explanations.explanation: The prophets don't come up in this passage, friend. The writer says God found fault with the people. That's the word that fits the blank.

explanations.answer: angels
explanations.explanation: Angels don't appear anywhere in this passage, friend. The writer says God found fault with the people. Leave the angels out of this one.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True, baker. God says, “…I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.” Those are His words, plain as day. Both houses are named.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That one's actually true. God says, “…I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.” He names both houses right there. Easy to doubt, though, when a promise this big shows up.

explanations.answer: They did not abide by it
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, “…they did not abide by My covenant…” That's why He says the new one won't be like it. It's a heavy line, and the text doesn't say more than that.

explanations.answer: They kept it for generations
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what God says. He says they did not abide by His covenant. Keeping it for generations would be a very different sentence.

explanations.answer: They renewed it every year
explanations.explanation: Renewing every year sounds like a subscription, but the text doesn't say that. God says the fathers did not abide by His covenant. That's the only thing He says they did with it here.

explanations.answer: In their minds and on their hearts
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says, “I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts.” The laws go on the inside. I think that's the part that gets me every time.

explanations.answer: On new tablets of stone
explanations.explanation: Stone tablets are real, friend. God gave Moses tablets of stone (Exodus 31:18). But in this new covenant, He says He will put His laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts.

explanations.answer: On the doorposts of their homes
explanations.explanation: Israel was told to write God's words on the doorposts of their houses (Deuteronomy 6:9). But that's not what God says about the new covenant here. He says He will put His laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts.

explanations.answer: He'll be their God and they'll be His people
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. God says, “And I will be their God, and they will be My people.” That's a relationship, not a roster. Short sentence, huge promise.

explanations.answer: He'll be their shield and they'll be His army
explanations.explanation: Shield and army sound strong, but God doesn't say that here. He says, “And I will be their God, and they will be My people.” That's the promise on the table.

explanations.answer: He'll be their King and they'll be His servants
explanations.explanation: That's a believable guess, friend, but it's not the wording. God says, “And I will be their God, and they will be My people.” Those are His words in this verse.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. God says, “…they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest.” That means all of them, the least and the greatest. Nobody is left out of the knowing.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right. God says, “…they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest.” It isn't only the greatest. Everybody in the covenant, from the least to the greatest, gets to know Him.

explanations.answer: He will remember them no more
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, “For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.” Forgiveness is the promise. Read it slowly, then read it again.

explanations.answer: He will count them one by one
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what God says. He promises to forgive their iniquities and remember their sins no more. No counting is mentioned.

explanations.answer: He will remember them for a season
explanations.explanation: A season would mean the sins are remembered for a time, and that's not what God says. He says He will remember their sins no more. “No more” leaves no season at all.

explanations.answer: It will soon disappear
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says, “…what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear.” He says it right after saying the new covenant made the first one obsolete. So the answer is right there in the verse: it will soon disappear.

explanations.answer: It will stand beside the new
explanations.explanation: Two covenants sharing one counter sounds cozy, friend, but that's not the picture here. The writer says what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear. He says it right after saying that by speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete. So the old doesn't stand beside the new, it disappears.

explanations.answer: It will be kept forever
explanations.explanation: Forever is a big word, friend, and the writer doesn't use it here. He says what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear. That's the end of the line for the old.
